analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 a month for people with private health insurance.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap insulin out-of-pocket costs at $35 a month for the roughly two-thirds of insulin users on private insurance never came up for a vote in the House or Senate, despite 102 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health plans and employer plans to cover at least one insulin of each major type, with no deductible and a copay of no more than $35 for a month's supply (or 25% of the negotiated price, if lower). It applies to plans starting in 2024 or later, including high-deductible and catastrophic plans. It would not change the list price insulin makers charge — only what patients pay at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private or employer insurance who use insulin and pay more than $35 a month out of pocket, including many on high-deductible plans who currently pay the full cash price until meeting their deductible. Payments under the cap would still count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, so patients would keep building toward their annual limit.

how_it_helps.text: Caps cost-sharing for a month's supply of covered insulin at $35 or 25% of the plan's negotiated price, whichever is lower, starting in 2024 [S2] [S3].
Applies the cap to group health plans, individual market plans, and high-deductible and catastrophic plans, and bars applying the deductible to covered insulin [S3].
Requires plans to cover at least one insulin product of each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) and each type (rapid-, short-, intermediate-, long-, ultra long-acting, and premixed) [S3].
Counts capped insulin payments toward the patient's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, so patients still progress toward their annual limit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurers and employer health plans would absorb the difference between what patients currently pay and the $35 cap, a cost that could flow into premiums for everyone with insurance. Insulin makers would not see their list prices capped, so any pressure on them would come indirectly, as plans and pharmacy benefit managers squeeze the negotiated price.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and other premium payers

drawbacks.text: The cap leaves drug list prices untouched, so it does not address the underlying reason insulin is expensive; plans would pick up the difference, and that cost could show up in premiums for everyone [S2] [S3].
Plans choose which insulin products count as 'selected,' so a patient's specific insulin might not be covered, and the cap does not apply to insulin obtained out-of-network [S3].

The cap excludes the uninsured and people on Medicare, who were covered separately by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act's Medicare insulin cap — the population left out is exactly the one this bill targets but does not finish covering.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of insured people who ration or skimp on insulin because of cost, a $35 monthly cap is a direct, meaningful saving. The trade-off is that the cost lands on insurers and employers rather than on drug makers' prices, and could nudge premiums up for everyone. It is a patient-cost fix, not a drug-price fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees and then to a health subcommittee, where it sat for the rest of the two-year Congress; neither chamber ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, with 102 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S4] [S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees, and later to a Health subcommittee; no committee ever voted on it and the House never brought it to the floor [S5].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without either chamber voting on it [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers, employers, and insulin manufacturers keep the status quo: no one had to absorb the cost of the cap or change how insulin is priced and sold, and insured patients paying more than $35 a month got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and insulin makers kept the status quo

industries.note: Plans would have to cover insulin with no deductible and cap patient cost-sharing at $35 a month, absorbing the difference themselves — a cost they could pass into premiums. Their interest in this bill runs against the patients the cap would help.

The bill does not cap what manufacturers charge; it works around their list prices by limiting what patients pay, so manufacturers keep their pricing power while plans and pharmacy benefit managers absorb the gap. High insulin list prices are the problem the bill treats the symptom of.

The cap's lower limit is calculated from the negotiated price 'net of all price concessions,' including those captured by pharmacy benefit managers — the bill builds the patient protection around the existing PBM system rather than changing it.
Self-insured employer plans are covered by the mandate and would bear part of the cap's cost, though many already offer $25–$35 insulin copays voluntarily.
